newsitem.title: UK: Loyalist leader moves to ease N.Irish crisis fear.
newsitem.headline: Loyalist leader moves to ease N.Irish crisis fear.

text.p: A politician linked to banned pro-British Loyalist guerrillas sought to calm fears on Monday that a booby-trap bomb attack on a senior Irish republican could plunge Northern Ireland into a new round of sectarian warfare.

BBC radio reported that the Loyalist Ulster Freedom Fighters (UFF) were thought to be responsible, but Protestant leader Gary McMichael said the incident might not signal the collapse of a two-year-old truce by guerrillas loyal to Britain.
Parties and Protestant and Catholic church leaders implored Loyalists not to propel the region into a spiral of conflict.

McMichael, who refused to condemn Sunday's explosion but stressed his opposition to all violence, said the guerrilla umbrella group, the Combined Loyalist Military Command, had not made any public comment about the attack.

"If the ceasefire was truly over I would have thought that they would have made a public pronouncement. That has not happened at this stage and I have not been given any indication privately that that would be the case," he told the BBC.
McMichael leads the Ulster Democratic Party, the political wing of the Ulster Defence Association -- like the UFF an outlawed Protestant extremist group.
Twenty-four hours after, no group had admitted the attack that injured Eddie Copeland, a 25-year-old Roman Catholic opposed to British rule over the province.

But politicians across the sectarian divide were convinced that Loyalists -- so called because they are "loyal" to British rule of Northern Ireland -- had mounted it as a reprisal for the wounding of a policeman by Irish Republican Army gunmen at a children's hospital last Friday.
The officer had been guarding a Protestant politician who was believed to be the target of the attack.

Political sources in Belfast said the Loyalist guerrillas, who called their truce in October 1994 in response to an IRA ceasefire, might have intended the attack as a one-off and might avoid any admission of responsibility that could lead to their political allies losing their seats in the peace talks.

A BBC report, which did not specify a source, said the bomb was believed to have been the work of a unit of the UFF based in the Shankill Road, Belfast's chief Protestant stronghold. It comprised a commercial detonator and an explosive substance, according to the report.

For 25 years the UFF waged a campaign killing residents in Irish Catholic neighbourhoods where the IRA draws support for its goal of an all-Ireland state. It and its UVF allies have been praised for sticking to their ceasefire even though the IRA broke its truce in February.
Bceause the IRA broke its truce, its Sinn Fein political wing is refused a seat in multi-party talks on the future of the province chaired by former U.S. senator George Mitchell.
Britain condemned the bombing but refused to say if it would mean the expulsion of Loyalist parties from peace talks.
"Whoever did this did a disgraceful and disgusting act and one which has to be unequivocally condemned," Britain's Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Patrick Mayhew told BBC radio.
